players.product: Triple Alpha quantum software development environment (hardware-agnostic compiler / deployment), run on an in-house quantum hardware testbed

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: Beryllium, Horizon's object-oriented quantum programming language (its highest level of abstraction currently available; classes, structs, scoped functions), is now available in early access; the company has built a standard set of libraries for it, including algorithmic building blocks such as a quantum Monte Carlo algorithm. Early access opened towards the end of the quarter, is still a relatively small group and is 'mostly hardware partners'; library development is so far primarily internal to Horizon.

CEO: the Ember-1 superconducting testbed system Horizon operates in Singapore has been opened to first users; integrating Triple Alpha directly with its control systems enables real-time execution of Hydrogen programs (its portable assembly language) without post-selection — loops, recursive function calls and concurrent classical function evaluation, plus real-time branching on measurement results, ingredients for real-time error correction. Horizon is still debugging parts of the system and seeing only initial feedback.

CEO: installation of Horizon's second testbed system is expected to start next year; it will be in Dublin, where Horizon is selecting a new office location (it is exceeding the space in its current Dublin office) and will build out lab facilities — giving it systems operating in both Singapore and Dublin.

CEO: Horizon is 'more limited by the capacity of our science and engineering teams rather than demand from the hardware companies to work with us'; it has interest from hardware manufacturers well below the Carbon layer, very good relationships with a wide range of hardware manufacturers, and is starting to work with a number of control systems manufacturers — 'we want to work with everyone'.

CEO: Horizon has established a quantum applications team focused on three specific high-value problems in each of three industries, doing the entire end-to-end development in-house (application through Triple Alpha, compilers and runtime down to its testbeds) rather than proof-of-concept work with industry; the existing AI / agentic-workflow team is being rolled into it. It is a long-term effort aimed at reaching real quantum advantage internally and driving adoption, not at applications to sell.

CEO: recent frontier AI models have started to yield real results in quantum information; Horizon has invested in AI systems with a dedicated team since 2023, and in the last few weeks its own agentic systems have produced hundreds of research notes on open problems in quantum computing — autonomous scientific discovery 'really potentially allows us to accelerate our roadmap'.

CEO: Horizon is building custom compilers so that developers and hardware collaborators can build their own compilation workflow with its tools, working towards an error correction library for different codes and compilation into fault-tolerant encodings; he notes industry-wide error correction is still very nascent.

CEO on competition: 'the real competition is classical compute'; other ways to program quantum computers exist (Qiskit from IBM, Classiq and others), but he sees Horizon's path of abstracting away the quantum mechanics to automatically accelerate classical code as unique. He says Horizon is tracking well against the milestones it set in the F-4.

CFO: Q2 2026 total operating expenses were approximately $7.2 million versus $2.8 million in Q2 2025; R&D approximately $2.6 million (up 117% from $1.2 million), sales and marketing approximately $0.38 million (up 51%), G&A approximately $3.8 million (up 236% from $1.1 million); loss from operations approximately $7.2 million; adjusted EBITDA loss approximately $5.5 million versus $2.1 million. Net loss was approximately $115.2 million ($2.20 per share), including a non-cash charge from remeasuring warrant-related derivative liabilities ($108 million per the CFO; $108.3 million per the CEO). CFO refers to the current pre-revenue period.
quarterly_data.figure: operating expenses ~$7.2 million; adjusted EBITDA loss ~$5.5 million; net loss ~$115.2 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: Q2 operating expenses are 'a reasonable base level' and 'a good base to look at in terms of expenses for the near term'. Horizon does not pursue proof-of-concept services work; it plans to engage in revenue generation when the quantum industry reaches quantum advantage, moving early-access users to paying users on a cost-per-use model, on the cloud or on-premise.

CFO: cash at the end of June 2026 was $113.3 million, up $16.7 million from $96.6 million at the end of March 2026; net cash used in operating activities was approximately $5.1 million in Q2 2026 (versus $2.0 million in Q2 2025 and $4.2 million in Q1 2026) and approximately $9.3 million in the first half (versus $3.7 million), mainly from headcount growth. He calls the software model capital-light; CEO says M&A is not a primary strategy.

CFO: Horizon ended Q2 2026 with 57 full-time employees versus 34 a year earlier (up 68%, up 10% sequentially); scientists, engineers and other technical staff remain within 60%-80% of total headcount, a mix expected to stay consistent.

CEO: Horizon announced a new collaboration with Quantum Machines aimed at developing embedded calibration - routines that run regularly in the background while the system operates, instead of a large batched calibration run at fixed intervals - for use in its Ember-1 testbed system in Singapore and potentially in other systems. Asked about possible future revenue from it: 'Potentially there is, but at the moment, we're focused on getting this working with our own system first.'
